1	# How a run works
2	
3	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
4	
5	A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
6	logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
7	scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
8	logins.
9	
10	## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
11	
12	RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.
13	
14	1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
15	   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
16	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
17	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
18	   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
19	   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
20	   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
21	   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
22	   provider takes your own key.
23	   Nothing done with these logins counts.
24	   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
25	2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
26	   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
27	   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
28	   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.
29	
30	## Inside a run
31	
32	1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
33	   returns:
34	   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
35	   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
36	   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
37	     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
38	   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
39	   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
40	   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
41	     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
42	   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
43	2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
44	   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
45	   provider's with your own key (below).
46	3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
47	   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
48	   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
49	   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
50	     it again.
51	   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
52	     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.
53	
54	Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
55	(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
56	front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.
57	
58	## LLM calls
59	
60	Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
61	Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
62	own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
63	API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.
64	
65	The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:
66	
67	```
68	$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
69	```
70	
71	`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:
72	
73	| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
74	| --- | --- | --- |
75	| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
76	| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
77	| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
78	| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
79	| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
80	| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
81	| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
82	| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
83	| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
84	| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |
85	
86	The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
87	each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
88	(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.
89	
90	### Your key
91	
92	Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
93	(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
94	unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
95	not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.
96	
97	With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
98	`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
99	as `x-api-key`:
100	
101	```python
102	from openai import OpenAI
103	
104	client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
105	```
106	
107	A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
108	the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:
109	
110	```python
111	import os
112	from google import genai
113	
114	client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
115	    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
116	```
117	
118	```javascript
119	import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"
120	
121	const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
122	  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
123	```
124	
125	A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
126	organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
127	key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
128	start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.
129	
130	**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
131	`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
132	(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
133	for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
134	`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
135	`401`.
136	
137	A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
138	context.
139	
140	### How cost is measured
141	
142	Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
143	provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
144	An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
145	`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
146	that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
147	a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
148	providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
149	chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
150	an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
151	early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
152	endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
153	fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.
154	
155	The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
156	charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.
157	
158	### Team secrets
159	
160	Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
161	`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:
162	
163	```sh
164	curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
165	  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
166	curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
167	curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
168	```
169	
170	Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
171	Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
172	cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
173	`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.
174	
175	## Scored run
176	
177	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
178	ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
179	[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
180	a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
181	`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:
182	
183	- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
184	- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
185	- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
186	  and the websites.
187	- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.
188	
189	1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
190	2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
191	   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
192	   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
193	   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
194	   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
195	   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
196	   right after setup:
197	
198	   ```json
199	   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
200	   ```
201	
202	   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
203	   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
204	   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.
205	
206	   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
207	   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
208	   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
209	   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
210	   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
211	   run that answered keeps its result.
212	3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.
213	
214	| Variable | Value |
215	| --- | --- |
216	| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
217	| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
218	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
219	| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
220	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
221	| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
222	| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
223	| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
224	| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
225	| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
226	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
227	| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
228	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
229	| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
230	| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
231	| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |
232	
233	The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
234	organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
235	run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
236	through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
237	ends without an answer scores 0.
238	
239	## Browsers
240	
241	The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:
242	
243	```json
244	{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
245	```
246	
247	`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
248	`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
249	own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
250	the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
251	them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:
252	
253	| Variable | Value |
254	| --- | --- |
255	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
256	| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
257	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |
258	
259	**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
260	inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
261	any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
262	`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
263	browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
264	recording of each afterwards.
265	
266	On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
267	browsers.

# How a run works

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
logins.

## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.

1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
   provider takes your own key.
   Nothing done with these logins counts.
   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.

## Inside a run

1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
   returns:
   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
   provider's with your own key (below).
3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
     it again.
   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.

Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.

## LLM calls

Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.

The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:

```
$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
```

`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:

| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |

The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.

### Your key

Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.

With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
as `x-api-key`:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
```

A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:

```python
import os
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
```

```javascript
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"

const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
```

A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.

**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
`401`.

A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
context.

### How cost is measured

Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.

The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.

### Team secrets

Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:

```sh
curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
```

Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.

## Scored run

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:

- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
  and the websites.
- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.

1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
   right after setup:

   ```json
   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
   ```

   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.

   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
   run that answered keeps its result.
3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |

The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
ends without an answer scores 0.

## Browsers

The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:

```json
{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
```

`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |

**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
recording of each afterwards.

On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
browsers.

1	# The CLI
2	
3	A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins. It is made for
4	people and coding agents alike: every command takes `--json`, and exit codes tell outcomes apart. Everything it does
5	is plain HTTP, described in the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md); you never need the CLI.
6	
7	## Install
8	
9	macOS and Linux:
10	
11	```sh
12	export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
13	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh
14	```
15	
16	Windows, in PowerShell (5.1 or 7):
17	
18	```powershell
19	$env:ATIRA_API = "https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai"
20	irm "$env:ATIRA_API/install.ps1" | iex
21	```
22	
23	The script checks for Node 24 or newer. Where it is missing, it asks whether to install a private copy for atira
24	alone, the latest Node 24 from nodejs.org, checked against the release's `SHASUMS256.txt`. It needs no admin rights
25	and never changes the `node` on your `PATH`. Without a terminal to ask in, `ATIRA_INSTALL_NODE=1` says yes (`0`, no).
26	Then it downloads `/cli.mjs`, checks it against `/cli.mjs.sha256` and installs it for you alone, without sudo:
27	
28	- macOS and Linux: the file in `~/.local/share/atira/atira.mjs`, Node (if needed) in `~/.local/share/atira/node`,
29	  and an `atira` command in `~/.local/bin`. It tells you when `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH`.
30	- Windows: the same under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira`, with `atira.cmd` in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira\bin`, which it adds to
31	  your user `PATH`. Open a new terminal afterwards.
32	
33	The `atira` command runs your own Node when it is 24 or newer, else the private copy. Running the installer again
34	updates the CLI; it downloads Node again only when the private copy is older than 24. Read the script first, if you
35	like:
36	
37	```sh
38	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
39	```
40	
41	To uninstall: `rm -rf ~/.local/share/atira ~/.local/bin/atira`, or on Windows
42	`Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\atira"`. Your sign-in stays in the config file (see below) until you
43	delete it.
44	
45	Without installing anything, download the file and run it with Node; `node atira.mjs` works wherever this guide
46	says `atira`:
47	
48	```sh
49	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
50	```
51	
52	The CLI talks to the server it was downloaded from. Set `ATIRA_API` to use another one. `atira upgrade` downloads the
53	server's current version, checks its SHA-256 and replaces the file; a download that does not match leaves the file
54	as it was.
55	
56	## Sign in
57	
58	```sh
59	atira login
60	```
61	
62	The browser opens a page that asks you to sign in with GitHub, then whether to sign in the CLI on this computer.
63	Approve, and the browser returns to the CLI, which stores a personal token for you. The token acts as you, on the
64	team you are in at the time of each request: leave the team, or be removed, and it no longer reaches the team. It
65	lasts 90 days. Your team page lists your signed-in devices; revoke any of them there.
66	
67	Where no browser can open (an SSH session, a container, a coding agent), sign in with a code instead:
68	
69	```sh
70	atira login --device
71	```
72	
73	It prints a link with the code filled in. Open it on any device, check that the code matches and approve; the CLI
74	waits and then stores the token. `atira login` switches to the code by itself when the browser cannot be opened, or
75	offers it when the browser has not answered after two minutes.
76	
77	```sh
78	atira whoami                                  # who you are, your team, and when the token expires
79	atira token                                   # the token, for curl and scripts
80	curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" "$ATIRA_API/v1/teams/me"
81	atira logout                                  # revoke the token on the server and forget it here
82	```
83	
84	The token is kept per server in `~/.config/atira/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atira/config.json`; on Windows
85	`%USERPROFILE%\.config\atira\config.json`), readable only by you (mode 0600). `ATIRA_TOKEN` overrides it, which suits
86	CI and agents: `export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)`.
87	
88	## Commands
89	
90	| Command | What it does |
91	| --- | --- |
92	| `login [--device] [--key <key>]` | Sign in through the browser, or with a code (`--device`), and store a personal token; `--key` stores a team key where there is no GitHub sign-in |
93	| `logout` | Revoke the stored token on the server and forget it |
94	| `whoami` | Who you are signed in as, your team, and when the token expires |
95	| `token` | Print the token in use, for `curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)"` |
96	| `upgrade` | Download the server's current CLI, check its SHA-256 and replace this file |
97	| `challenges` | The challenges, with their Markdown pages |
98	| `challenge <id>` | A challenge as Markdown: task, websites, rules, run contract, submitting, answer schema |
99	| `scout [--challenge <id>] [--env [--port <port>]]` | The published scouting logins for the public websites; `--env` prints them as shell exports for running your agent locally, with any hosted model's variables pointed at `atira models proxy`; use the same `--port` when the proxy runs on another port |
100	| `models proxy [--port <port>]` | Where the organizers host models: a local proxy to them on 127.0.0.1 (port 8765) that prints each model's base URL and key variables |
101	| `test-run <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset and open its run page; `--follow` prints its place in the queue, then streams its logs here |
102	| `submit <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder and submit it: review, then one scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page; `--follow` prints the review, each run's place in the queue and its end here |
103	| `cancel <run>` | Cancel a test or scored run that has not finished: its sandbox is removed and the run fails |
104	| `final [--best-of <1\|3>] [--challenge <id>]` | Read or change the final attempt choice before the final run starts |
105	| `status [<id>] [--challenge <id>]` | Your latest submissions and test runs, or one submission (`sub_...`), test run (`reh_...`) or run (`run_...`) |
106	| `logs <run> [--follow]` | A test or scored run's logs; `--follow` keeps polling until the run has ended |
107	| `package <id> [--out <dir>]` | The package a test run (`reh_...` or `run_...`), scored run or submission (`sub_...`) of your team used, as uploaded: agent.json and each file's size; `--out` saves the `.tar.gz` in a folder, checked against its SHA-256 |
108	| `leaderboard [--challenge <id>]` | The leaderboard |
109	| `mcp` | Serve MCP on stdio for your coding agent: list and debug runs (why one failed, logs by time, model calls, where the time went, a browser's screen at a time, recorded inputs, two runs compared), start and wait for test runs, and cancel a run or submit when you confirm ([MCP guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md)) |
110	
111	Every command accepts `--json` (machine-readable output on stdout, errors included) and `--help`.
112	`--challenge` defaults to `ATIRA_CHALLENGE`, else the platform's first challenge. While `login` waits, it writes its
113	instructions to stderr, so `--json` output on stdout stays one JSON document.
114	
115	### Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
116	
117	Develop against the public websites on your own machine, then test the package in the sandbox:
118	
119	```sh
120	atira scout                    # the scouting logins: each website, its URL, username and password
121	eval "$(atira scout --env)"    # the same as shell exports
122	uv run python agent.py         # your agent, on your machine, against the public websites (the starter kit's way)
123	atira test-run ./my-agent      # then one run in the sandbox, opened live in the browser
124	```
125	
126	On Windows, `--env` and `models proxy` print PowerShell's `$env:NAME = '...'` instead; load them with
127	`atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`.
128	
129	### Hosted models from your machine
130	
131	Where the organizers host models, a run gets each one's base URL and key variables set for it, and the
132	Getting started page names them. On your machine, run the proxy in its own terminal: it prints the same variables,
133	pointed at itself, with `local` as the key (any non-empty value works through it).
134	
135	```sh
136	atira login                    # once per computer
137	atira models proxy             # keep it running; it prints the exports
138	```
139	
140	`eval "$(atira scout --env)"` sets the same variables with the scouting logins; it never exports your sign-in. The proxy
141	listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It holds a 30-minute inference token, good for model calls only and bound to an Ed25519 key
142	that never leaves the process, signs every call with that key and rotates the token before it expires. A copied token
143	works in no other client. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. If port 8765 is in use, pick
144	the same port for the proxy and the scouting exports:
145	
146	```sh
147	atira models proxy --port 8777                   # in a second terminal
148	eval "$(atira scout --env --port 8777)"
149	```
150	
151	In PowerShell, the second line is `atira scout --env --port 8777 | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`. The proxy also
152	prints the command with its actual port, including when `--port 0` lets the operating system choose one.
153	
154	`scout` needs no sign-in for the logins. It prints the logins the organizers published, how long they are valid,
155	and what happens to an answer: these are demo logins, so an answer entered on the website that takes it is
156	acknowledged without counting. For RFQ, a bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting. `--json` prints what
157	`GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returns: the logins as `access`, plus `submission`, `brief` and `answer_schema`,
158	shaped like a run's `/v1/runs/current`. `--env` prints:
159	
160	| Variable | Value |
161	| --- | --- |
162	| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING` | what `GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returned, as JSON: the brief, logins and answer format |
163	| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` | `$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/<id>/scouting`, the same without a token once the organizers publish the logins |
164	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with the scouting logins, the JSON a run gets: `[{"siteId", "url", "credentials": {"username", "password"}}]` |
165	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL` | each website's URL, its id upper-cased with `_` for other characters, e.g. `CHALLENGE_SITE_TENDER_PORTAL_URL` |
166	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | only when the platform hosts models: each one through `atira models proxy` on this computer, with `local` as the key. Keep the proxy running in another terminal, signed in with `atira login`. `atira scout --help` names them |
167	
168	With `--env --json`, the same variables come as one JSON object. There is no run token: your agent calls other
169	models with your own key, directly or through the model proxy with your personal token (see
170	[LLM calls](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)). Calls through the proxy from your machine, a hosted model's included, are
171	recorded for your team and never ranked. A hosted model is free to use, never charged; each call counts toward your
172	run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest. Nothing done with these logins counts.
173	Locally there are no browsers from the platform (`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `DISPLAY`) and no egress
174	proxy: your agent starts its own browsers. When nothing is published yet, `scout` exits 4: organizers publish the scouting logins before the event.
175	
176	### Test runs and submissions
177	
178	```sh
179	atira test-run ./my-agent --dry-run   # what would be uploaded, and what is left out
180	atira test-run ./my-agent             # one run in the sandbox on the public dataset; opens its run page
181	atira test-run ./my-agent --follow    # the same, and its logs here until it ends
182	atira cancel run_...                  # stop a run that has not finished
183	atira submit ./my-agent               # review, then the scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page
184	atira status sub_...
185	```
186	
187	`test-run` uploads the package, starts the test run and, when its output goes to a terminal, opens the run page in
188	the browser: the browser, the logs, the phases and the score with its full breakdown, live. `submit` opens your team
189	page instead, which shows the submission's review and then links each scored run as it starts: the run does not
190	exist until the review has passed, which takes minutes, so the CLI does not wait for it unless you pass `--follow`.
191	`ATIRA_BROWSER` picks the
192	command that opens the page (`none` only prints the link), `--no-open` skips it, and `--json` never opens anything.
193	
194	`test-run --follow` then streams the run's logs as `logs --follow` does and exits 7 if the run failed or timed out.
195	While the run waits for a sandbox, it prints its place in the [fair queue](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#the-run-queue) on stderr whenever
196	that changes ("Queued: 3 runs ahead of yours"). With `--json --follow`, the upload's result comes as one JSON line,
197	then one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` line per chunk. `submit --follow` prints the review's outcome, then each scored
198	run's place in the queue and its end, and exits 7 unless the submission completes; with `--json`, the final
199	submission follows the upload's line.
200	
201	`cancel <run>` takes a run (`run_...`) or a test run (`reh_...`) of your team that has not finished. The run's sandbox
202	is removed and the run fails with the error "Cancelled by @you"; a queued run is cancelled before it starts. Your
203	team can start the next test run at once. A cancelled scored run leaves its submission not complete: the leaderboard
204	ignores that submission, and you can submit again. A run that
205	has already finished answers 409 (exit 6).
206	
207	`test-run` and `submit` pack the folder into a gzipped tarball the way the platform reads it:
208	
209	- `agent.json` must be at the folder's root, with `run` (and optionally `setup`) as arrays of strings.
210	- `.git`, `node_modules` and `.DS_Store` are always left out, and so is whatever `.gitignore` files exclude (in the
211	  folder and below: patterns, `*`, `?`, `**`, `[...]`, a leading `/`, a trailing `/` for folders, and `!` to
212	  include again). Symbolic links are left out too.
213	- The limits are checked before uploading: at most 2,000 files, 5 MB per file, 20 MB in total, and 20 MB
214	  compressed (or what the server announces).
215	
216	### Logs, status and the leaderboard
217	
218	`package <id>` shows exactly what a run ran: the package's SHA-256 and label, its `agent.json` and every file with
219	its size. A scored run ran its submission's package. `--out ./downloaded` also saves the `.tar.gz` there; unpack it
220	with `tar -xzf <file> -C <folder>`.
221	
222	`logs <run>` prints what the run has written so far; `--follow` polls with a growing pause (1 s, up to 10 s) and
223	exits when the run has ended. `--json` prints one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` object per line. `status` without an id
224	shows your best result, your latest submissions and your latest test runs.
225	
226	## Configuration
227	
228	| Variable | Meaning |
229	| --- | --- |
230	| `ATIRA_API` | The platform; defaults to the server the file came from |
231	| `ATIRA_TOKEN` | A token to use instead of the stored one |
232	| `ATIRA_CHALLENGE` | The default challenge |
233	| `ATIRA_POLL_MS` | The first pause of `logs --follow`, in milliseconds (default 1000) |
234	| `ATIRA_BROWSER` | The command `login`, `test-run` and `submit` open pages with, or `none` to only print the link |
235	| `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | Where `atira/config.json` lives (default `~/.config`) |
236	
237	The config file holds `{"servers": {"<ATIRA_API>": {"token": "atp_...", "token_id", "expires_at", "login"}}}`.
238	
239	## Exit codes
240	
241	| Code | Meaning |
242	| --- | --- |
243	| 0 | Done |
244	| 1 | Network or server error |
245	| 2 | Usage: unknown command or option, a missing argument, a folder that does not exist |
246	| 3 | Not signed in, sign-in cancelled or expired, or the server refused the credential (401, 403) |
247	| 4 | Not found (404) |
248	| 5 | Invalid request or package: a missing `agent.json`, over a limit, a 400 or 413 |
249	| 6 | Busy: a submission already in evaluation, 3 test runs already waiting, a rate limit, or cancelling a finished run (409, 429) |
250	| 7 | `logs --follow` or `test-run --follow`: the run failed or timed out; `submit --follow`: the submission did not complete |
251	
252	With `--json`, an error is printed as `{"error": {"code", "message", "status"}}` on stdout.

255	
256	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
257	page or with `atira final --best-of 3` before the final run starts. Your best attempt counts. Details:

# The CLI

A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins. It is made for
people and coding agents alike: every command takes `--json`, and exit codes tell outcomes apart. Everything it does
is plain HTTP, described in the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md); you never need the CLI.

## Install

macOS and Linux:

```sh
export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh
```

Windows, in PowerShell (5.1 or 7):

```powershell
$env:ATIRA_API = "https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai"
irm "$env:ATIRA_API/install.ps1" | iex
```

The script checks for Node 24 or newer. Where it is missing, it asks whether to install a private copy for atira
alone, the latest Node 24 from nodejs.org, checked against the release's `SHASUMS256.txt`. It needs no admin rights
and never changes the `node` on your `PATH`. Without a terminal to ask in, `ATIRA_INSTALL_NODE=1` says yes (`0`, no).
Then it downloads `/cli.mjs`, checks it against `/cli.mjs.sha256` and installs it for you alone, without sudo:

- macOS and Linux: the file in `~/.local/share/atira/atira.mjs`, Node (if needed) in `~/.local/share/atira/node`,
  and an `atira` command in `~/.local/bin`. It tells you when `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH`.
- Windows: the same under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira`, with `atira.cmd` in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira\bin`, which it adds to
  your user `PATH`. Open a new terminal afterwards.

The `atira` command runs your own Node when it is 24 or newer, else the private copy. Running the installer again
updates the CLI; it downloads Node again only when the private copy is older than 24. Read the script first, if you
like:

```sh
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
```

To uninstall: `rm -rf ~/.local/share/atira ~/.local/bin/atira`, or on Windows
`Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\atira"`. Your sign-in stays in the config file (see below) until you
delete it.

Without installing anything, download the file and run it with Node; `node atira.mjs` works wherever this guide
says `atira`:

```sh
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
```

The CLI talks to the server it was downloaded from. Set `ATIRA_API` to use another one. `atira upgrade` downloads the
server's current version, checks its SHA-256 and replaces the file; a download that does not match leaves the file
as it was.

## Sign in

```sh
atira login
```

The browser opens a page that asks you to sign in with GitHub, then whether to sign in the CLI on this computer.
Approve, and the browser returns to the CLI, which stores a personal token for you. The token acts as you, on the
team you are in at the time of each request: leave the team, or be removed, and it no longer reaches the team. It
lasts 90 days. Your team page lists your signed-in devices; revoke any of them there.

Where no browser can open (an SSH session, a container, a coding agent), sign in with a code instead:

```sh
atira login --device
```

It prints a link with the code filled in. Open it on any device, check that the code matches and approve; the CLI
waits and then stores the token. `atira login` switches to the code by itself when the browser cannot be opened, or
offers it when the browser has not answered after two minutes.

```sh
atira whoami                                  # who you are, your team, and when the token expires
atira token                                   # the token, for curl and scripts
curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" "$ATIRA_API/v1/teams/me"
atira logout                                  # revoke the token on the server and forget it here
```

The token is kept per server in `~/.config/atira/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atira/config.json`; on Windows
`%USERPROFILE%\.config\atira\config.json`), readable only by you (mode 0600). `ATIRA_TOKEN` overrides it, which suits
CI and agents: `export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)`.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `login [--device] [--key <key>]` | Sign in through the browser, or with a code (`--device`), and store a personal token; `--key` stores a team key where there is no GitHub sign-in |
| `logout` | Revoke the stored token on the server and forget it |
| `whoami` | Who you are signed in as, your team, and when the token expires |
| `token` | Print the token in use, for `curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)"` |
| `upgrade` | Download the server's current CLI, check its SHA-256 and replace this file |
| `challenges` | The challenges, with their Markdown pages |
| `challenge <id>` | A challenge as Markdown: task, websites, rules, run contract, submitting, answer schema |
| `scout [--challenge <id>] [--env [--port <port>]]` | The published scouting logins for the public websites; `--env` prints them as shell exports for running your agent locally, with any hosted model's variables pointed at `atira models proxy`; use the same `--port` when the proxy runs on another port |
| `models proxy [--port <port>]` | Where the organizers host models: a local proxy to them on 127.0.0.1 (port 8765) that prints each model's base URL and key variables |
| `test-run <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset and open its run page; `--follow` prints its place in the queue, then streams its logs here |
| `submit <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder and submit it: review, then one scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page; `--follow` prints the review, each run's place in the queue and its end here |
| `cancel <run>` | Cancel a test or scored run that has not finished: its sandbox is removed and the run fails |
| `final [--best-of <1\|3>] [--challenge <id>]` | Read or change the final attempt choice before the final run starts |
| `status [<id>] [--challenge <id>]` | Your latest submissions and test runs, or one submission (`sub_...`), test run (`reh_...`) or run (`run_...`) |
| `logs <run> [--follow]` | A test or scored run's logs; `--follow` keeps polling until the run has ended |
| `package <id> [--out <dir>]` | The package a test run (`reh_...` or `run_...`), scored run or submission (`sub_...`) of your team used, as uploaded: agent.json and each file's size; `--out` saves the `.tar.gz` in a folder, checked against its SHA-256 |
| `leaderboard [--challenge <id>]` | The leaderboard |
| `mcp` | Serve MCP on stdio for your coding agent: list and debug runs (why one failed, logs by time, model calls, where the time went, a browser's screen at a time, recorded inputs, two runs compared), start and wait for test runs, and cancel a run or submit when you confirm ([MCP guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md)) |

Every command accepts `--json` (machine-readable output on stdout, errors included) and `--help`.
`--challenge` defaults to `ATIRA_CHALLENGE`, else the platform's first challenge. While `login` waits, it writes its
instructions to stderr, so `--json` output on stdout stays one JSON document.

### Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

Develop against the public websites on your own machine, then test the package in the sandbox:

```sh
atira scout                    # the scouting logins: each website, its URL, username and password
eval "$(atira scout --env)"    # the same as shell exports
uv run python agent.py         # your agent, on your machine, against the public websites (the starter kit's way)
atira test-run ./my-agent      # then one run in the sandbox, opened live in the browser
```

On Windows, `--env` and `models proxy` print PowerShell's `$env:NAME = '...'` instead; load them with
`atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`.

### Hosted models from your machine

Where the organizers host models, a run gets each one's base URL and key variables set for it, and the
Getting started page names them. On your machine, run the proxy in its own terminal: it prints the same variables,
pointed at itself, with `local` as the key (any non-empty value works through it).

```sh
atira login                    # once per computer
atira models proxy             # keep it running; it prints the exports
```

`eval "$(atira scout --env)"` sets the same variables with the scouting logins; it never exports your sign-in. The proxy
listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It holds a 30-minute inference token, good for model calls only and bound to an Ed25519 key
that never leaves the process, signs every call with that key and rotates the token before it expires. A copied token
works in no other client. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. If port 8765 is in use, pick
the same port for the proxy and the scouting exports:

```sh
atira models proxy --port 8777                   # in a second terminal
eval "$(atira scout --env --port 8777)"
```

In PowerShell, the second line is `atira scout --env --port 8777 | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`. The proxy also
prints the command with its actual port, including when `--port 0` lets the operating system choose one.

`scout` needs no sign-in for the logins. It prints the logins the organizers published, how long they are valid,
and what happens to an answer: these are demo logins, so an answer entered on the website that takes it is
acknowledged without counting. For RFQ, a bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting. `--json` prints what
`GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returns: the logins as `access`, plus `submission`, `brief` and `answer_schema`,
shaped like a run's `/v1/runs/current`. `--env` prints:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING` | what `GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returned, as JSON: the brief, logins and answer format |
| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` | `$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/<id>/scouting`, the same without a token once the organizers publish the logins |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with the scouting logins, the JSON a run gets: `[{"siteId", "url", "credentials": {"username", "password"}}]` |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL` | each website's URL, its id upper-cased with `_` for other characters, e.g. `CHALLENGE_SITE_TENDER_PORTAL_URL` |
| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | only when the platform hosts models: each one through `atira models proxy` on this computer, with `local` as the key. Keep the proxy running in another terminal, signed in with `atira login`. `atira scout --help` names them |

With `--env --json`, the same variables come as one JSON object. There is no run token: your agent calls other
models with your own key, directly or through the model proxy with your personal token (see
[LLM calls](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)). Calls through the proxy from your machine, a hosted model's included, are
recorded for your team and never ranked. A hosted model is free to use, never charged; each call counts toward your
run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest. Nothing done with these logins counts.
Locally there are no browsers from the platform (`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `DISPLAY`) and no egress
proxy: your agent starts its own browsers. When nothing is published yet, `scout` exits 4: organizers publish the scouting logins before the event.

### Test runs and submissions

```sh
atira test-run ./my-agent --dry-run   # what would be uploaded, and what is left out
atira test-run ./my-agent             # one run in the sandbox on the public dataset; opens its run page
atira test-run ./my-agent --follow    # the same, and its logs here until it ends
atira cancel run_...                  # stop a run that has not finished
atira submit ./my-agent               # review, then the scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page
atira status sub_...
```

`test-run` uploads the package, starts the test run and, when its output goes to a terminal, opens the run page in
the browser: the browser, the logs, the phases and the score with its full breakdown, live. `submit` opens your team
page instead, which shows the submission's review and then links each scored run as it starts: the run does not
exist until the review has passed, which takes minutes, so the CLI does not wait for it unless you pass `--follow`.
`ATIRA_BROWSER` picks the
command that opens the page (`none` only prints the link), `--no-open` skips it, and `--json` never opens anything.

`test-run --follow` then streams the run's logs as `logs --follow` does and exits 7 if the run failed or timed out.
While the run waits for a sandbox, it prints its place in the [fair queue](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#the-run-queue) on stderr whenever
that changes ("Queued: 3 runs ahead of yours"). With `--json --follow`, the upload's result comes as one JSON line,
then one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` line per chunk. `submit --follow` prints the review's outcome, then each scored
run's place in the queue and its end, and exits 7 unless the submission completes; with `--json`, the final
submission follows the upload's line.

`cancel <run>` takes a run (`run_...`) or a test run (`reh_...`) of your team that has not finished. The run's sandbox
is removed and the run fails with the error "Cancelled by @you"; a queued run is cancelled before it starts. Your
team can start the next test run at once. A cancelled scored run leaves its submission not complete: the leaderboard
ignores that submission, and you can submit again. A run that
has already finished answers 409 (exit 6).

`test-run` and `submit` pack the folder into a gzipped tarball the way the platform reads it:

- `agent.json` must be at the folder's root, with `run` (and optionally `setup`) as arrays of strings.
- `.git`, `node_modules` and `.DS_Store` are always left out, and so is whatever `.gitignore` files exclude (in the
  folder and below: patterns, `*`, `?`, `**`, `[...]`, a leading `/`, a trailing `/` for folders, and `!` to
  include again). Symbolic links are left out too.
- The limits are checked before uploading: at most 2,000 files, 5 MB per file, 20 MB in total, and 20 MB
  compressed (or what the server announces).

### Logs, status and the leaderboard

`package <id>` shows exactly what a run ran: the package's SHA-256 and label, its `agent.json` and every file with
its size. A scored run ran its submission's package. `--out ./downloaded` also saves the `.tar.gz` there; unpack it
with `tar -xzf <file> -C <folder>`.

`logs <run>` prints what the run has written so far; `--follow` polls with a growing pause (1 s, up to 10 s) and
exits when the run has ended. `--json` prints one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` object per line. `status` without an id
shows your best result, your latest submissions and your latest test runs.

## Configuration

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ATIRA_API` | The platform; defaults to the server the file came from |
| `ATIRA_TOKEN` | A token to use instead of the stored one |
| `ATIRA_CHALLENGE` | The default challenge |
| `ATIRA_POLL_MS` | The first pause of `logs --follow`, in milliseconds (default 1000) |
| `ATIRA_BROWSER` | The command `login`, `test-run` and `submit` open pages with, or `none` to only print the link |
| `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` | Where `atira/config.json` lives (default `~/.config`) |

The config file holds `{"servers": {"<ATIRA_API>": {"token": "atp_...", "token_id", "expires_at", "login"}}}`.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Done |
| 1 | Network or server error |
| 2 | Usage: unknown command or option, a missing argument, a folder that does not exist |
| 3 | Not signed in, sign-in cancelled or expired, or the server refused the credential (401, 403) |
| 4 | Not found (404) |
| 5 | Invalid request or package: a missing `agent.json`, over a limit, a 400 or 413 |
| 6 | Busy: a submission already in evaluation, 3 test runs already waiting, a rate limit, or cancelling a finished run (409, 429) |
| 7 | `logs --follow` or `test-run --follow`: the run failed or timed out; `submit --follow`: the submission did not complete |

With `--json`, an error is printed as `{"error": {"code", "message", "status"}}` on stdout.

## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three

The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
page or with `atira final --best-of 3` before the final run starts. Your best attempt counts. Details:
[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).

1	# Submitting
2	
3	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
4	
5	You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball. We review it, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset
6	and score it. That run determines its rank on the leaderboard. When the hackathon ends, your latest submission that
7	passed review runs once more, on a private dataset, in the [final run](#what-happens-next), which weighs most when we pick the winners.
8	
9	## Package layout
10	
11	```
12	agent.json          {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": ["qwen"]}
13	pyproject.toml      (or package.json, requirements.txt, ...)
14	agent.py            your code
15	```
16	
17	- `agent.json` at the root: `setup` (optional) and `run`, each an argv array. Both run in the package directory.
18	  `browsers` (optional, 1 to 4, default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts for the run; see
19	  [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#browsers). `models` (optional) lists the hosted models your agent system calls,
20	  by provider id, all of them by default: the run's clock waits for those to warm up, and `[]` starts it right after
21	  setup; see [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#scored-run).
22	- At most 20 MB compressed; regular files only.
23	- No secrets: the run gets everything it needs from the environment.
24	
25	## Upload
26	
27	```
28	tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
29	curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
30	  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
31	  $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions
32	```
33	
34	The response (`202`) has your submission's id. Review is still pending and no runs exist yet: follow it with
35	`GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions` for the review result and run ids, or watch the leaderboard.
36	
37	`$ATIRA_TOKEN` is your personal token: `atira login` signs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) in through the browser, and
38	`atira token` prints the token (or sign in with plain curl, as the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in) shows).
39	
40	Or let the CLI pack, check and upload the folder: `atira submit my-agent` (and `atira test-run my-agent` for a
41	test run). It leaves out `.git`, `node_modules` and what `.gitignore` excludes. In a terminal, `submit` then opens
42	your team page, which shows the review and links each scored run as it starts, and `test-run` opens the run page.
43	
44	## Test it in the sandbox first
45	
46	Upload the same tarball as a test run ("Test runs" on your team page, or
47	`POST $API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals` with the same headers). It runs once in the scored-run sandbox against
48	the public scenario `public-1`, scored with the points for each part of the answer. Its live view shows the
49	browser (a frame about every 1.5 s, or the live screen where available), the phases, every model call,
50	and your logs as the agent prints them. Afterwards the recorded video stays available to
51	your team. Up to 4 test runs at a time per team. `atira test-run my-agent` uploads it, starts the run
52	and opens it live; `atira cancel` (or Cancel run on the run page) stops a run that has not finished, and frees its
53	test-run slot at once.
54	
55	## Linking your GitHub repository
56	
57	The organizers ask each team to link the GitHub repository it builds its agent in, so they can review the
58	code, for example to compare a winning submission with its source. On your team page, the captain chooses
59	Connect a GitHub repository, installs the organizers' GitHub App on the account that owns the repository
60	(granting it only that repository is enough), and picks the repository. Every member sees the linked repository,
61	who linked it and when; the captain can switch or unlink it at any time.
62	
63	The app only reads the contents of the repositories you grant it; it cannot push, open issues or change
64	settings. Linking does not change how you submit: scored submissions and test runs are still the tarballs
65	described above. To withdraw access completely, unlink the repository and uninstall the app in your GitHub
66	settings.
67	
68	## Watching your submission
69	
70	Each scored run has a live view with its phase, timer, model calls, tokens and cost. On the public dataset it also
71	shows your team the browser (frames, and the live screen where available), the logs and errors
72	unredacted and the scenario id, and the recording afterwards. The final run on the private dataset shows its
73	screen, frames and recordings to the organizers only; your team reads its logs and errors with private values
74	masked as `[private]`.
75	
76	## Resubmitting
77	
78	Submit as often as you like, one at a time: while a submission is still in review or has unfinished runs, the
79	next upload is refused with `429`. Your **best complete** submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
80	**latest** one that passed review goes into the final run. Your other submissions stay in your history at
81	`$API/team`. Cancelling a submission's scored run ends that submission: it never completes, the leaderboard ignores it, and you
82	can submit again.
83	
84	## What happens next
85	
86	1. **Review:** passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged submission still runs and scores, but its result
87	   stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it marked
88	   "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Your team sees the outcome, not the reviewer's reasons. The organizers can
89	   still pass or disqualify a submission later; a disqualified one reads "disqualified", leaves the leaderboard and
90	   the final run, and your team page gives the organizers' reason.
91	2. **Scored run:** one run in a fresh sandbox on the public dataset, setup first (up to 5 minutes, not counted),
92	   then your run command (timed).
93	3. **Ranking:** once the run has finished and review is passed, your submission appears on the leaderboard with its quality, cost and
94	   time; ineligible answers rank after every eligible one.
95	4. **Final run:** when the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review
96	   (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected and disqualified ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. It is the latest one, not the best one.
97	   That run weighs most when we pick the winners ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to
98	   the public scenario. Its results stay with the organizers until they publish them; then the leaderboard shows
99	   the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", and the public-dataset board stays at
100	   `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`.
101	
102	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
103	
104	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
105	page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:
106	[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).
